content.title: Solving Systems of Linear Equations: Substitution, Elimination, and Graphing
content.overview: This guide covers the three core methods for solving systems of two linear equations: substitution, elimination, and graphing. Mastering these methods is fundamental to solving complex problems in the SAT Algebra section.
learning_objectives: Understand and apply the substitution method to solve systems
Understand and apply the elimination method (addition/subtraction) to solve systems
Understand the relationship between intersection points and solutions in the graphing method
Select the most efficient solving strategy based on the characteristics of the system

sections.title: Substitution Method
sections.content: Substitution involves choosing one equation to express one variable in terms of the other, then substituting that expression into the second equation. This method is best when a variable in one equation has a coefficient of 1 or -1. Steps: 1. Isolate: Solve for x or y in one equation. 2. Substitute: Plug this expression into the other equation to eliminate a variable. 3. Solve: Solve the resulting single-variable equation. 4. Back-substitute: Plug the value back into the isolated equation to find the other variable.

sections.title: Elimination Method
sections.content:
Elimination (also known as the addition/subtraction method) involves adding or subtracting the two equations to eliminate one variable. If the coefficients are not equal, multiply one or both equations by a constant first. Steps: 1. Align: Ensure x-terms, y-terms, and constants are aligned. 2. Adjust Coefficients: Multiply to make the coefficients of one variable either identical or opposites. 3. Add or Subtract: Combine the equations to eliminate the variable. 4. Solve and back-substitute.

![Standard Elimination Method Process](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/00b9409c-e365-4172-b318-c7ae6560bc29-1786502029989-302.webp)

sections.title: Graphing Method
sections.content: On the coordinate plane, the solution to a system of linear equations corresponds to the coordinates $(x, y)$ of the intersection point of the two lines. If the lines intersect, the coordinates of that point are the unique solution. While manual graphing has limited precision on the SAT, understanding the logic is vital for determining the existence of solutions.

worked_examples.question:
Solve the system:
1) $y = 2x - 3$
2) $3x + 2y = 8$
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Since equation 1 already provides an expression for y, use substitution. Substitute $y = 2x - 3$ into equation 2.
Step 2: $3x + 2(2x - 3) = 8$.
Step 3: Expand and combine like terms: $3x + 4x - 6 = 8 \rightarrow 7x = 14 \rightarrow x = 2$.
Step 4: Substitute $x = 2$ back into equation 1: $y = 2(2) - 3 = 1$.
Result: The solution is $(2, 1)$.

worked_examples.question:
Solve the system:
1) $4x + 3y = 10$
2) $2x - 3y = 8$
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Observe that the coefficients of y are opposites (3 and -3), so use elimination.
Step 2: Add the two equations: $(4x + 2x) + (3y - 3y) = 10 + 8$.
Step 3: $6x = 18 \rightarrow x = 3$.
Step 4: Substitute $x = 3$ into equation 2: $2(3) - 3y = 8 \rightarrow 6 - 3y = 8 \rightarrow -3y = 2 \rightarrow y = -2/3$.
Result: The solution is $(3, -2/3)$.

common_mistakes: Substitution Errors: Forgetting to use parentheses when substituting an expression, leading to sign errors (especially with subtraction).
Wrong Elimination Direction: Subtracting when coefficients are opposites or adding when they are identical; this fails to eliminate the variable.
Solving for only one variable: Finding x but forgetting to find y, or entering the wrong variable in a grid-in question.
exam_tips: If a variable is already isolated (e.g., $y = ...$), prioritize the substitution method.
If the variables are aligned and coefficients are proportional, prioritize the elimination method.
The SAT often asks for the value of $x + y$ or $x - y$; check if you can get this directly by adding or subtracting equations without solving for x and y individually.
Use calculator functions (if permitted) to verify intersection coordinates.
content.recap: The key to solving systems is 'elimination'—turning a two-variable problem into a one-variable problem. Substitution is ideal for isolated variables, elimination is ideal for aligned coefficients, and graphing provides the geometric interpretation: the solution is the intersection.

knowledge_claims.content: A solution to a system of linear equations is a set of values $(x, y)$ that makes all equations in the system true simultaneously.
The first step of substitution is usually rearranging one equation to express one variable in terms of the other.
In elimination, if the coefficients of a variable are identical in both equations, subtract the equations to eliminate that variable.
In elimination, if the coefficients of a variable are opposites in both equations, add the equations to eliminate that variable.
On a coordinate plane, the solution to a system of two linear equations corresponds to the intersection point of the two lines.
When using substitution, failing to use parentheses for an expression preceded by a negative sign or coefficient leads to calculation errors.
After finding a solution $(x, y)$, it should be substituted back into both original equations to verify it satisfies both.
Substitution is generally more convenient than elimination when the coefficient of one variable is 1 or -1.
Before using elimination, ensure that like terms (x-terms, y-terms) are aligned on the same side of the equals sign.
If a question asks for $x + y$, try adding the equations directly to see if $(x + y)$ can be factored out as a single unit to save time.
